newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo talks show Asian markets maturing -- analyst.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo talks show Asian markets maturing -- analyst.

text.p: A meeting of senior finance and central bank officials from five Asian economies and the United States to be held on Tuesday highlights the growing importance of Asian financial markets, a senior economist said on Monday.

Officials from the United States, Japan, Australia, China, Singapore and Hong Kong will meet in Tokyo for a day of talks on cooperation in financial markets, macroeconomic policy and other matters of common concern.

"I'm sure they have a lot of important things to discuss but I suspect it is mostly an information exchange meeting," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia. "It is a recognition of the coming of age of Asian markets."

U.S. and Japanese officials have appeared keen to play down expectations that the gathering, dubbed by some media an Asian "Group of Six" but officially called the "Six Markets Meeting," will produce much more than talk at first.

Among the topics seen on the agenda are ways to improve cooperation in financial markets, macroeconomic policies, financial industry supervision and possible responses in the event of an Asian version of the Mexican financial crisis.

"The main aim is to create a forum for the exchange of information about financial and capital markets," said Mikio Wakatsuki, a former senior official at the Bank of Japan, in an interview with financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun.

"In particular, Japan has in the past tended to look toward Europe and the United States and has not had much of a channel for the exchange of information with financial authorities in the Asian region. This will likely be a good chance for Japan to create such communication channels," Wakatsuki said.
Japanese officials have stressed the importance of having in the new forum both China, a growing economic powerhouse, and the United States, whose currency dominates the region.
"The United States probably considers this a chance to create a relationship of better understanding with China," Wakatsuki was quoted as saying.

Among the participants will be U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers and U.S. Federal Reserve Board member Laurence Meyer. Japan will be represented by Vice Finance Minister for International Affairs Takatoshi Kato and Akira Nagashima, deputy governor for international relations at the Bank of Japan.

Summers will also hold a series of talks on Tuesday with Japanese officials including Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, Kato, and Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the ministry's International Finance Bureau.

Summers grabbed currency market attention on Friday when he warned Japan against trying to export its way out of its economic problems and urged it to restore domestic demand-led growth and repair its financial system.
